# Praise of *Alchemy*.

The following *rhymes* / which are very precious and good / I have wished to place here / And although the *author* did not *observe* the *meter* <note>The rhythmic structure or poetic measure of the verses.</note>, I have nonetheless not wished to *correct* them / so that the *author’s* meaning might not be changed.

I confess and declare /
That we have five fires /
The first pure / *Pure* / and almighty /
In its being eternal and powerful /
The <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "fünffte wesen," referring to the *Quinta Essentia* or Quintessence, the purest and most concentrated medicinal or spiritual force in alchemy.</note> of all things /
From which the whole world springs /
Makes blessed / powerful and rich /
Gives poverty and damns at the same time /
Sends out 4 beams upon the world.
From which one counts four more fires /
They are hot within / and cold without /

## Praise of *Alchemy*.

They transform themselves into the form of water.
The Philosophers <note>Referring to the "Alchemical Philosophers" or adepts of the art.</note> can *coagulate* <note>To solidify a liquid substance into a solid or semi-solid state.</note> it,
And transform it into *crystalline salt* /
Quite bright and clear / like moonlight /
At that point it is pure and clean /
Yet one must take great care.
That from three fires, one is made
Through its *resolving* <note>The process of dissolving or breaking a substance down into its component parts.</note>,
And transform it into *crystalline salt* /
Thus I speak here openly /
That a *particular* <note>In alchemy, a "particular" refers to a process that improves specific metals rather than the "universal" transformation of all matter.</note> is nevertheless more /
Only understand the true foundation /
By which the *metals* become healthy /
A leprosy <note>original: "Aussatz." Alchemists viewed the impurities in base metals as a disease like leprosy that needed to be cured to reach the "health" of gold.</note> is in their <term>sulphur</term> <note>original: "Sulphure." In alchemical theory, Sulphur represents the principle of combustibility, soul, and oily quality within matter.</note> /
Therefore <note>original: "Ergò"</note>, cure sulphur with sulphur, that is my cunning skill /
Sulphur, a fire / make that into salt /
Pure / fine, and fluid like melted fat /
When such three fires are united /
Then you have truly a *stone* <note>Referring to the Philosopher’s Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note> /
Which can cure your leprosy /
And set it aside before everyone /
Yet *humility* should be alongside this /

## Praise of *Alchemy*. <note>original: "Alchymiæ."</note>

So I will give you the three fires /
And reveal where they are,
Say "yes" once and never "no,"
The first fire is God the Lord,
From whom we have all teachings.
The other three in one sum:
<term>Salt</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>, <note>original: "Sal, Sulphur vnd Mercurium." These are the "Three Primes" (Tria Prima) of Paracelsian alchemy, believed to be the basic components of all matter.</note>
These three are animal,
Vegetable, and mineral;
Within these lies the foundation
By which the metals become healthy. <note>In alchemical thought, base metals were seen as "sick" or "leperous" versions of gold; the alchemist's task was to "heal" them into perfection.</note>
Therefore, proceed rightly,
So that you correctly follow my teaching,
And thank God, you Christians,
And avoid all <term>sophists</term>. <note>In this context, "sophists" refers to fraudulent alchemists who lacked spiritual insight and only performed "tricks" with chemistry.</note>
Yet another fire is at hand;
The same is quite immense
(Yet cheap and not expensive).
This same fire, I tell you, my son, <note>OCR ends at "Soh," likely "Sohn" (son).</note>
Is volatile, powerful, intensely wondrous, <note>OCR ends at "wunderse," likely "wunderseltsam" (wondrously strange).</note>
Fast as the wind / a flee[ing] <note>OCR ends at "flüch," likely "flüchtig" (volatile or fleeing).</note>
->Child,<-
In the belly of the wind, where you [find] it. <note>OCR ends at "f," likely "findest" (find). This is a famous reference to the "Emerald Tablet," an ancient alchemical text which states: "The wind carried it in its belly."</note>

# Praise of *Alchemy*. <note>original: "Alchymiæ."</note>

The strongest strength, I say truly,
Is revealed in this Fire;
It is not a fire like any other fire,
Yet it is no fire bought dearly with money; <note>Alchemists often claimed that the "matter" of the Great Work was common, cheap, and found everywhere—even in waste—contrasting it with the expensive reagents used by fraudulent "puffers."</note>
It is found in all places,
Among the poor, the rich, and the wretched.
A wind of wind, its true child;
Also the Sun and Moon are its parents; <note>This is a direct paraphrase of the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational alchemical text. It describes the "Stone" as having the Sun for its father, the Moon for its mother, and being carried by the wind.</note>
The four elements and the fine stars
Must all be submissive to it.
Also all metals and precious stones
Must go to ruin before it.
Yes, the fire made from gold
Has brought this fire to ashes,
Wherewith the children of Israel
Were watered and cured quickly
Of their sins, which they [committed] against God
When they danced around the calf with great mockery. <note>In the Book of Exodus, Moses destroys the Golden Calf by burning it and grinding it into powder, which he then makes the Israelites drink. Alchemists interpreted this as a high-level chemical process to create "Potable Gold," a universal medicine.</note>
Through [the knowledge] God gave to Moses,
So that the children of Israel kept their lives;
Otherwise they would have had to face death,
Lost in the pains of Hell.
Therefore this fire is found...

# Praise of *Alchemy*. <note>original: "Alchymiæ," the Latin genitive or dative form of Alchemy.</note>

And what is joined herewith/
That becomes stable entirely and completely/
Much sooner than in a year/
Makes pure and clean the <term>life-blood</term>/ <note>original: "Geblüt." In early modern medicine, "Geblüt" referred not just to blood, but to the entire system of humors and the vitality of the body.</note>
When it has received its redness/ <note>This refers to the "Rubedo" or Reddening, the final stage of the Alchemical Great Work, signaling the completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>
No illness can remain before it
For it cures everyone/
<term>Leprosy</term>/ <term>Gout</term> <note>original: "Podagra," a specific term for gout in the feet.</note> and <term>Dropsy</term> <note>original: "Wassersucht," an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>

->I.<-

# THE SECRET
## OF ALL SE-
### CRETS.

->That is:<-

## Concerning the Secrecy of All Secrets.

# Preface.

Since I have undertaken to write and produce a small book concerning the <term>transformation<note>original: *Verenderung*. In an alchemical context, this refers to the transmutation of base metals into noble ones like gold or silver.</note></term> and manifold <term>multiplication<note>original: *Vermehrung*. This is a specific alchemical process intended to increase the potency or quantity of a transmuting agent.</note></term> of metals, divided into eleven general chapters regarding their <term>generation<note>original: *generation*. This refers to the early scientific and alchemical theory that metals "grow" or are born deep within the earth like plants or embryos.</note></term> and growth, and [have intended] to present the same to Your Holiness and high wisdom, not only to read, but also to oversee, correct, and improve.

I have, for the sake of brevity, knowingly and deliberately [passed over] the obstacles in this <term>Art<note>The "Art" (German: *Kunst*) is a standard historical term for the practice of alchemy.</note></term>—those pertaining to the body, the soul, and other occurrences of accidental events—

<summary>The author introduces his eleven-chapter treatise on the alchemical growth and transmutation of metals, dedicating the work to a high-ranking figure ("Your Holiness") for scholarly review.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, transmutation, multiplication of metals, mineral generation, preface, Your Holiness, alchemical art</keywords>

->Preface.<-

...events and unfortunate conditions and more of the like, through which the <term>Work<note>original: *Arbeit*. In alchemical literature, "the Work" (or *Opus*) refers to the specific experimental procedures required to achieve transmutation or the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term> might be diverted from this noble end, [we] will not introduce here, because they are dealt with in other places. Likewise, for the sake of the intended brevity, we do not wish to dispute with the ignorant and the <term>sophists<note>original: *Sophisten*. A term used by alchemists to describe those who argue using empty logic or "false" philosophy without practical or spiritual understanding of the Art.</note></term>—some of whom completely deny the <term>Art<note>original: *Kunst*. In the first chapter, the <term>matter<note>original: *Materia*. In this context, it refers to the primary physical substance or "base" of the metals before they are transformed.</note></term> of metals and their natural essence is taught.

In the second chapter, [the book treats] of the active and proper causes of metals in general.

In the third, of the natural <term>principles<note>original: *Principiis*. In early modern science and alchemy, these are the fundamental components—typically salt, sulfur, and mercury—that Nature uses to build all matter.</note></term> and origin upon which Nature bases its work.

In the fourth, of the <term>artful essence<note>original: *kunstreichen Wesen*. This refers to the properties of metals as they relate to the "Art" (alchemy), particularly how they are understood through human skill and laboratory practice.</note></term> of metals.

The Alchemists’ teaching, according to the opinion of the ancient **philosophers**, says: That the natural <term>principles</term> <note>original: *principia*; the fundamental starting materials or components in alchemical theory.</note>—the beginning of the work of Nature—are **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original symbol: ☿; also known as mercury.</note>. For we see that many and various arts are invented, and each achieves its effect through its appropriate instrument; it is the same for those who wish to change <term>matters</term> <note>original: Materias; the raw substances used in alchemical work</note> through burning, cooking, and <term>digestion</term> <note>original: digestion; the process of maturing a substance through gentle, consistent heat, often compared to incubation</note>.

### The Fifth Chapter

...resolved to say something about these operations. Therefore I say that the Philosophers have established many works—such as **sublimation**, **distillation**, **descension**, and **creation**—out of envy <note>intentional obfuscation used by alchemists to hide their secrets from the uninitiated</note>, so that the art might be obscured. For you should know that when our **Stone** is in our vessel and feels our **Sun** <note>the heat of the furnace or the active sulfurous principle</note>, it is immediately dissolved into water. This water rises to the top into the upper part of the vessel and thereafter falls again to the bottom of the same; and one should know that our **matter** rises through smoke and air.

And when the Philosophers say that the matter rises and falls through the smoke and wind, they deliberated on what they should call the work. They agreed that they would call these first risings the first **sublimation** <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collects as a solid or liquid</note>. Afterwards, when they saw that the matter fell again to the base or bottom of the vessel and turned into water, they decided in their hearts and called it the first **solution** <term>solution</term> <note>the dissolving of a solid into a liquid state</note>. As they then saw this rising and falling, which made the matter into <term>water</term> <note>original: ▽, the alchemical symbol for water</note>, they named such **distillation** as the third work and **descension** as the fourth.

There is, however, also another **Mercury** <term>☿</term> that is called living silver <note>quicksilver</note>, of which **Geber** <term>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century alchemist whose writings formed the basis of medieval chemistry</term> says: that it contains much superfluous watery moisture, earthly putrefaction <note>original: *Faulheit*</note>, and impurity, which must be separated from it through **sublimation** <term>the process of heating a substance into vapor and then solidifying it again to purify it</term>. # On the Power and Final Effect or Utility of the Medicine, as well as what Alchemy, the Stone, or the Elixir may be.

### The Eleventh Chapter.

Blessed be the Lord God forever, who has given such power to mankind that man may be a follower of nature, change natural things, and—through the cooperation of nature—create such a medicine <note>original: *Artney*</note> with Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art" or "Great Work" by practitioners.</note>, that he may preserve metallic bodies <note>In alchemy, "metallic bodies" often refers both to literal metals being purified and to the human body, which was thought to contain "metallic" or mineral spirits.</note> from their future infirmities and keep them in fresh youth; thus is the most secret, noble mystery accomplished in this world as an inexhaustible and intangible treasure.

Therefore, my dear children of wisdom <note>original: *Kinder der Weißheit*. But you, children of wickedness, flee from this Art, for it is contrary to you and will leave you stuck in poverty and misery; and know that this worthy and noble gift is entirely hidden and denied to you.

### The Lily Among the Thorns.
<note>original: "Lilium inter spinas." A biblical reference to the Song of Solomon 2:2, often used in alchemical and mystical literature to represent the pure truth or the "Philosopher's Stone" found amidst the difficulties and "thorns" of worldly matter.</note>

The laudable and high **GOD** has, according to His manifold grace, given abundant understanding to those so that they might fear Him and walk in His commandments. This same **God** has, out of Fatherly love, made and created man after His own image <note>original: "Ebenbild"</note>; and not only that, but He also made subject to him all creatures which He created for man's benefit. And what is even more, He breathed His spirit into that same man and made him immortal. For the sake of this immortality, man was granted the power to distinguish good from evil, and also to know the nature of all things and the hidden causes of every elemental thing <term>elementirten Dings; refers to anything composed of the four classical elements: earth, air, fire, and water</term>. Among other wonders, the metallic creations are excellent, which are so thoroughly hidden from man that even a researcher of natural things—who is called a **Philosopher** <term>Philosophus; in this context, a "natural philosopher" or an early scientist and alchemist</term>—can hardly fathom <note>The text ends mid-word with "außgrün-," likely for "ausgründen" (to fathom or investigate deeply).</note>

### The Lily Among the Thorns.
<note>original: "Lilium inter spinas." A biblical reference to the Song of Solomon 2:2, commonly used in alchemical texts to signify the pure, noble "lily" of the Philosopher's Stone hidden within the "thorns" of crude matter.</note>

For how can it be—and why is it—that the Earth, which in its depths is cold and dry, gives birth to and brings forth the elements of the metals, such as **Gold**, **Silver**, **Mercury**, **Saturn**, **Venus**, and **Mars** <note>represented in the original by symbols: Sol ☉, Luna ☽, ☿, ♄, ♀, and ♂</note>, as well as various imperfect things, such as all kinds of **marcasite** <term>marcasit; a term used then for various iron-sulfide minerals often mistaken for or associated with metal ores</term> and **antimony**? In all these things, however, an obvious warmth and moisture is discovered, which each possesses according to its own degree, much or little, as is well known to anyone who researches the nature of metals. For there is no doubt that **Gold** possesses both moisture and warmth in a perfectly balanced proportion, while **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> is cold and moist, and **Mars** <note>Iron</note> is cold and dry.

Although the **Philosophers** <term>Philosophi; here meaning natural philosophers or alchemists who study the physical world</term> say that through the power of natural warmth, which passes through the veins of the earth, the **cooking of metals** <term>Kochung der Metallen; the "digestion" or maturation process believed to happen underground over geological time</term> takes place—and that such a thing is hardly accomplished in many thousands of years—yet **Almighty GOD** has granted to man, as His most noble creature on earth, the gift of natural **Art** to anticipate such a long time. This is done through "naturing nature" <note>original: "genaturte Natur," likely referring to the concept of *natura naturata*, or nature acting according to its inherent laws</note>. And **God** has revealed such Art to His "little ones" <note>a reference to humble, pious seekers rather than the prideful</note> and endowed them with such understanding; so that, where Nature requires a long duration, they may accomplish the same in a short time through Art.

[poi]-sonous <note>Completing the word from the previous page: "poisonous"</note> animals; also in such places grow poisonous herbs, such as <term>Napellus</term> <note>Also known as Monkshood or Aconite, a famously deadly plant in historical pharmacology</note> and many others of the kind; and such things derive their poisonous nature from nowhere else than that they do not have good, fresh, healthy air. Now we shall see how the earth (as our <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus, the foundational authorities of alchemical theory</note> says) is to be abundantly increased with the air. Note then: it is necessary that there be more of the air than of the <term>Water</term> <note>original symbol: ▽</note>. The reason is this: there are 2 degrees of cold in the <term>composition</term> <note>The alchemical mixture or "Great Work" in progress</note>—one from the earth, the other from the water. Now the air, which is warm in one degree (for we shall remain silent about the other quality <note>Air is considered both Warm and Moist; the author is focusing only on the temperature balance here</note>), must be added to the <term>composition</term> in such quantity until the two degrees of cold agree with the warmth of the air and become equal. # A Good Foundation or Good Treatise on the Philosopher’s Stone.

One should take half an ounce <note>original: "℥", the symbol for an ounce</note> of the purified volatile stone, and of the fixed stone—that is, of the fixed <term>Sulphur</term> <note>original: "Sulphuræ"; in alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle</note>—a third part of an ounce, and of the stone of the Earth, a fourth part of an ounce. This vessel should be made in the likeness of a mother’s womb, or the shape of an **egg** <note>The "Philosopher’s Egg" is a sealed container that allows for circular distillation, where steam rises and falls back down without escaping.</note>. ## Here begins the Book of the Key of the Treasures.
### And is the first chapter.

Although the philosophers <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers specifically to the alchemists of antiquity and the Middle Ages who sought the secrets of nature.</note> have written books without number, and have also composed beautiful and lovely poems with elegant, hidden sayings regarding the art of Alchemy <note>original: *Alchmia*</note>; and the philosophers call this art a true, proven, and a Divine Art, and they regard and prize it above all other arts as the nearest [to truth], the highest, and the most noble, second only to the art of Astronomy, which is the mother of all lesser arts. For it is even named with the name of its mother, Astronomy, and is called "Lower Astronomy" <note>This term reflects the Hermetic belief that the properties of metals and earthly substances are the terrestrial counterparts to the stars and planets (Upper Astronomy).</note>. Such is also its operation...

Alchemy is deeply founded and proven; he [Johannes von Dettschin] himself made and possessed the highest <term>Stone of the Philosophers <note>The goal of the "Great Work," believed to transform base metals into gold and grant spiritual perfection.</note></term> through the grace of God and his own manual labor. In his rhymed verses <note>original: *metra*</note>, the art is entirely revealed and sufficiently disclosed without any "envy" <note>Alchemists often used the term "envy" to describe the practice of intentionally hiding secrets from the uninitiated. But through the "Key" of Rupecissa <note>Referring to the 14th-century Franciscan alchemist Jean de Roquetaillade, whose work serves as the interpretive guide for this text.</note>, all his writings and teachings are explained and recognized.

Thus, there will be three parts: **fix** <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</term> one part, and keep the other two parts. I will explain it even better: take the Stone of our **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: in alchemy, this is not the modern chemical, but a name for the "primal matter" or a specific mineral thought to contain the essence of the Stone.</term> and separate from it the most pure substance—that is our **Key**. Divide the other part again into two parts. **Fix** and **coagulate** <term>Coagulation: the solidification or thickening of a liquid substance.</term> one part. With the other kept part, **dissolve**, **impregnate**, and wash or "sweat" it. With the third part, **incerate** <term>Inceration: a process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency.</term>—that is, with the third kept part, make this fixed and dry **Matter** liquid and increase it thereby until it flows in the fire before the **Mercury** <note>In this context, the volatile spirit or the "soul" of the metal.</note> vanishes. Thus you have fulfilled the work with honor.

## This is the first work.

Take common salt and Roman vitriol <note>Roman vitriol typically refers to copper sulfate, which appears as blue crystals.</note>, 2 pounds of each; grind them finely and dry them well in an earthen basin. Stir the mixture constantly over a gentle <term>fire</term> <note>The triangle symbol △ represents the element of Fire.</note> until the watery moisture evaporates. After that, take 1 pound of <term>mercury</term> <note>The symbol ☿ represents Mercury, or quicksilver.</note> and place it into a double-layered cloth, or parchment, or a piece of leather. Squeeze the mercury through the cloth or leather into the basin while the material is still somewhat warm. As it strains through the pores of the leather, press and stir the material with a wooden spatula; the material will then absorb the mercury into itself until it is no longer visible.

Then, place this into a <term>sublimation vessel</term> <note>original: "sublimatorium"; a specialized glass or ceramic container used to heat a solid until it becomes vapor and then collects as a purified solid at the top.</note> to be sublimated. Begin first with a gentle fire until the moisture escapes through the opening at the top; you can detect this by placing a metal plate over the opening, etc. Afterward, seal the opening with <term>lute</term> <note>original: "Leime"; a specialized alchemical paste or clay used to hermetically seal vessels.</note>, though it is safer to ensure the material is thoroughly dried beforehand so that no opening needs to remain. Increase the fire for 12 hours, and at the very end, provide a stronger fire so that all of the mercury is sublimated.

Then, let it cool overnight. When you take it out, it will be sublimated as white as snow. In this sublimated mercury resides the red Spirit of Vitriol <note>The "Spirit of Vitriol" refers to the acidic vapors (sulfuric acid precursors) released during heating, which react with the mercury and salt to create "corrosive sublimate" (mercuric chloride).</note>, which is called

### The Fourth Work

After the <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a fine powder.</note> has been completed for us, as previously described, in the dry chamber, place that same Spirit into a sealed or closed vessel of <term>vitriol</term> <note>A sulfate-based chemical, often used here to refer to the acidic environment created within the vessel.</note> in a <term>bain-marie</term> <note>original: "Balneum"; a water bath used for gentle, even heating.</note> in a pot full of water until the Spirit is entirely dissolved into water. ## The Sixth Work.

In the sixth work, I learn to bring this Stone—which has now been brought to the white stage—further toward the Red stage, with absolutely nothing added or taken away. Take the vessel out of the furnace, which is called the <term>Philosophers’ Egg</term> <note>original: "Ovum Philos:"; an oval-shaped glass vessel used to symbolize the "incubation" of the Stone.</note>, etc. Master Arnold <note>Likely Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist whose works were highly influential.</note> says that the Stone is enclosed within it just as Christ was in His tomb. From that same white matter, take one part, as much as you wish, and grind it into a subtle, intangible powder. Keep this, so that with it you may transmute all imperfect metals into good silver—better even than the natural kind. 

The other part, seal again in a glass vessel like the first one was, and strengthen the fire gently, as Master Arnold commands, who says: after the Stone comes to the perfect whiteness, it no longer fears the punishment of the roasting or burning fire. It is also not harmful if the fire is strengthened, though only to a moderate degree, as is proper and necessary for it. The reason for this is truly that the gentle warmth used during the cooking of the white Stone would not be able to <term>digest</term> <note>original: "tigeriren" / "geriren"; to cook, mature, or process the substance through heat.</note>

The Mercury of the Alchemists <note>original Latin: "Mercurius Alchimistarum." The internal "fire" or "grease" of a metal that allows it to be transformed or multiplied.</note>

This superfluity hinders the digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturing a substance through gentle, consistent heat.</note> so that the matter cannot reach its perfection.

Now the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy itself.</note> consists in this: that the superfluity be separated from the pure matter <note>original Latin: "materia pura"</note>; only then can the pure matter be digested toward its perfect ripening <note>original Latin: "maturatio"</note>.

But how this comes to pass is proven by the LIGHT of Nature <note>original Latin: "LUMEN Naturæ"; a Paracelsian term referring to the innate wisdom or divine spark within the natural world that guides growth and understanding.</note>: namely, that there must be an essential fire, just as is proven through the heat of Nature and of the Sun <note>original Latin: "calorem Naturæ & Solis"</note>, which ripens all generated things in the greater world <note>original Latin: "majori mundo"; the macrocosm or the universe at large.</note> and separates the impurities from the pure. To say it in a word, it is an essential fire <note>original Latin: "ignis essentialis"</note> of the same origin as the transmutable subject <note>original Latin: "cum subjecto transmutabili"</note>.

For all things that contribute to the generation and corruption <note>The Aristotelian cycle of coming into being ("generation") and passing away ("corruption").</note> of any natural individual must agree in matter of the same kind.

->I have spoken.<- <note>original Latin: "Dixi"; a traditional authoritative closing.</note>

<summary>The author explains that base metals are simply "impure" versions of gold, hindered by "extraneous sulfur," and argues that alchemical transformation requires an "essential fire" modeled after the sun’s natural ripening power.</summary>

Praised be **GOD**, who, after such long-lasting darkness, gloom, and black storm clouds, has joyfully caused His bright daylight—the beloved **Sun**—to rise.

However, the **Sun**, which is positioned in the middle between **Heaven** and **Earth**, is the clearest **Body** <term>Corpus; a physical or celestial entity</term> among all those in the entire world. Through it, the Heavens—which are immeasurable to human eyes—communicate and bestow their light and radiance upon all other stars and subordinate bodies. 

With its overwhelming power and clarity, the **Sun** not only visibly suppresses and shuts away the malice, false appearances, and tyranny of its hovering enemies—namely the most scorching **Mars** <note>original symbol: ♂</note>, the falsely-glimmering **Jupiter** <note>original symbol: ♃</note>, and the coldest **Saturn** <note>original symbol: ♄</note>—but also dominates them to such an extent that it receives its power from **Heaven** unhindered, and can provide and extend it to the lower world without being harmed by them. > From Him I ask to be taught much more which I do not know, from whom I have received the few things I do know; I ask Him that, with His <term>mercy (misericordia): the compassionate grace of God</term> going before and following after, He may teach me whatever things ought to be known for salvation which I do not know. In those things which I have known to be true, may He preserve me. In those in which I, as a human, am mistaken, may He correct me; in those truths where I am certain, may He confirm me, and from false and harmful things, may He deliver me. Amen, Amen. <note>original: "A quo postulo doceri multo plura, quæ nescio, à quo accepi pauca quæ scio, Ipsum rogo, ut præveniente & subsequente misericordia, quæcunq; salubriter scienda nescio, doceat me. In hisquæ vera novi, custodiat me. In quibus ut homo fallor, corrigat me; in quibus veris titulo confirmet me, & à falsis & noxiis eripiat me, Amen, Amen."</note>

# Alchemy

Neander, Theophilus, *Heptas Alchymica* <note>Greek/Latin: "Alchemical Sevenfold."</note> That is: Select Philosophical Treatises on the **Mastery of the Stone** <note>original: "Magisterio Lapidis," referring to the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, which belong as a completion to the *Promptuarium Alchymiae* <note>Latin: "Alchemical Storehouse" or "Handbook."</note> of the late, distinguished Master Dr. Joachim Tanck, former Professor at the laudable University of Leipzig, and which serve for a clear understanding of the preceding books and are necessary, and have not previously been seen in open print. But now produced and brought to light for the honor of the noble art of Alchemy, as well as for the benefit of the **sons and disciples of Hermes** <note>original: "filiis und discipulis Hermeticis." A traditional term for students of alchemy, referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. With 1 half-page woodcut. 8 leaves, 430 (mistakenly 130) pages. Small octavo. Marbled paper boards of the 18th century with a spine label. Halle (P. Schmidt) for H. Gross in Leipzig, 1621.
<insert>2800.</insert>

---

In the preface, the editor explains that the treatises summarized here were "assigned" by Tanck (died 1609) to complete his *Promptuarium*; he himself only reviewed them. Following writings by anonymous authors, Johannes Trithemius <note>A famous Benedictine abbot and polymath known for his work in cryptography and magic.</note>, and Johannes de Padua, pages 241-259 contain "On the Philosopher's Stone,"

the 10th Treatise of the *Archidoxorum* <note>Latin: "The Archidoxes," or "The Great Secrets."</note> of Paracelsus the Great and pages 261-293 *Liber Clavis Thesaurorum* <note>Latin: "The Book of the Key of Treasures."</note>. Here begins the **Book of the Key of Treasures**.

> "References to this book are few. It is quoted by
> Lenglet Dufresnoy and by Gmelin, who is careful to
> distinguish the author from Michael Neander, who
> wrote Syntagma, a sort of history of medicine... Curi-
> ously enough the 'Heptas alchymica' has escaped
> Kopp's notice, though he enumerates other collect-
> ions of seven tracts. I have found nothing about
> the compiler" (Ferguson II, 132).

Margins of the title page partially reinforced, likewise the bottom margin of leaf 2. Evenly browned throughout. — Very rare!
